go_terms.name: transcription coregulator activity
go_terms.definition: A transcription regulator activity that modulates the transcription of specific gene sets via binding to a DNA-binding transcription factor at a specific genomic locus, either on its own or as part of a complex. Coregulators often act by altering chromatin structure and modifications. For example, one class of transcription coregulators modifies chromatin structure through covalent modification of histones. A second class remodels the conformation of chromatin in an ATP-dependent fashion. A third class modulates interactions of DNA-bound DNA-binding transcription factors with other transcription coregulators.

go_terms.name: transcription coactivator activity
go_terms.definition: A transcription coregulator activity that activates or increases the transcription of specific gene sets via binding to a DNA-binding transcription factor at a specific genomic locus, either on its own or as part of a complex. Coactivators often act by altering chromatin structure and modifications. For example, one class of transcription coactivators modifies chromatin structure through covalent modification of histones. A second class remodels the conformation of chromatin in an ATP-dependent fashion. A third class modulates interactions of DNA-bound DNA-binding transcription factors with other transcription coregulators. A fourth class of coactivator activity is the bridging of a DNA-binding transcription factor to the general (basal) transcription machinery. The Mediator complex, which bridges sequence-specific DNA binding transcription factors and RNA polymerase, is also a transcription coactivator.

go_terms.name: mediator complex
go_terms.definition: A protein complex that interacts with the carboxy-terminal domain of the largest subunit of RNA polymerase II and plays an active role in transducing the signal from a transcription factor to the transcriptional machinery. The mediator complex is required for activation of transcription of most protein-coding genes, but can also act as a transcriptional corepressor. The Saccharomyces complex contains several identifiable subcomplexes: a head domain comprising Srb2, -4, and -5, Med6, -8, and -11, and Rox3 proteins; a middle domain comprising Med1, -4, and -7, Nut1 and -2, Cse2, Rgr1, Soh1, and Srb7 proteins; a tail consisting of Gal11p, Med2p, Pgd1p, and Sin4p; and a regulatory subcomplex comprising Ssn2, -3, and -8, and Srb8 proteins. Metazoan mediator complexes have similar modular structures and include homologs of yeast Srb and Med proteins.

go_terms.name: spliceosomal complex
go_terms.definition: Any of a series of ribonucleoprotein complexes that contain snRNA(s) and small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs), and are formed sequentially during the spliceosomal splicing of one or more substrate RNAs, and which also contain the RNA substrate(s) from the initial target RNAs of splicing, the splicing intermediate RNA(s), to the final RNA products. During cis-splicing, the initial target RNA is a single, contiguous RNA transcript, whether mRNA, snoRNA, etc., and the released products are a spliced RNA and an excised intron, generally as a lariat structure. During trans-splicing, there are two initial substrate RNAs, the spliced leader RNA and a pre-mRNA.

go_terms.definition: Any of the long, generally straight, hollow tubes of internal diameter 12-15 nm and external diameter 24 nm found in a wide variety of eukaryotic cells; each consists (usually) of 13 protofilaments of polymeric tubulin, staggered in such a manner that the tubulin monomers are arranged in a helical pattern on the microtubular surface, and with the alpha/beta axes of the tubulin subunits parallel to the long axis of the tubule; exist in equilibrium with pool of tubulin monomers and can be rapidly assembled or disassembled in response to physiological stimuli; concerned with force generation, e.g. in the spindle.

go_terms.name: chemical synaptic transmission

This process encompasses both spontaneous and evoked release of neurotransmitter and all parts of synaptic vesicle exocytosis. Evoked transmission starts with the arrival of an action potential at the presynapse.

go_terms.name: substantia nigra development
go_terms.definition: The progression of the substantia nigra over time from its initial formation until its mature state. The substantia nigra is the layer of gray substance that separates the posterior parts of the cerebral peduncles (tegmentum mesencephali) from the anterior parts; it normally includes a posterior compact part with many pigmented cells (pars compacta) and an anterior reticular part whose cells contain little pigment (pars reticularis).

go_terms.name: myelin sheath
go_terms.definition: An electrically insulating fatty layer that surrounds the axons of many neurons. It is an outgrowth of glial cells: Schwann cells supply the myelin for peripheral neurons while oligodendrocytes supply it to those of the central nervous system.

go_terms.name: synapse
go_terms.definition: The junction between an axon of one neuron and a dendrite of another neuron, a muscle fiber or a glial cell. As the axon approaches the synapse it enlarges into a specialized structure, the presynaptic terminal bouton, which contains mitochondria and synaptic vesicles. At the tip of the terminal bouton is the presynaptic membrane; facing it, and separated from it by a minute cleft (the synaptic cleft) is a specialized area of membrane on the receiving cell, known as the postsynaptic membrane. In response to the arrival of nerve impulses, the presynaptic terminal bouton secretes molecules of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft. These diffuse across the cleft and transmit the signal to the postsynaptic membrane.

go_terms.name: extracellular exosome
go_terms.definition: A vesicle that is released into the extracellular region by fusion of the limiting endosomal membrane of a multivesicular body with the plasma membrane. Extracellular exosomes, also simply called exosomes, have a diameter of about 40-100 nm.

go_terms.name: endoplasmic reticulum
go_terms.definition: The irregular network of unit membranes, visible only by electron microscopy, that occurs in the cytoplasm of many eukaryotic cells. The ER takes two forms, rough (or granular), with ribosomes adhering to the outer surface, and smooth (with no ribosomes attached).

go_terms.name: DNA repair
go_terms.definition: The process of restoring DNA after damage. Genomes are subject to damage by chemical and physical agents in the environment (e.g. UV and ionizing radiations, chemical mutagens, fungal and bacterial toxins, etc.) and by free radicals or alkylating agents endogenously generated in metabolism. DNA is also damaged because of errors during its replication. A variety of different DNA repair pathways have been reported that include direct reversal, base excision repair, nucleotide excision repair, photoreactivation, bypass, double-strand break repair pathway, and mismatch repair pathway.

go_terms.name: synapse
go_terms.definition: The junction between an axon of one neuron and a dendrite of another neuron, a muscle fiber or a glial cell. As the axon approaches the synapse it enlarges into a specialized structure, the presynaptic terminal bouton, which contains mitochondria and synaptic vesicles. At the tip of the terminal bouton is the presynaptic membrane; facing it, and separated from it by a minute cleft (the synaptic cleft) is a specialized area of membrane on the receiving cell, known as the postsynaptic membrane. In response to the arrival of nerve impulses, the presynaptic terminal bouton secretes molecules of neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft. These diffuse across the cleft and transmit the signal to the postsynaptic membrane.

go_terms.definition: The series of molecular signals initiated by a ligand binding to its receptor, in which the activated receptor promotes the exchange of GDP for GTP on the alpha-subunit of an associated heterotrimeric G-protein complex. The pathway begins with receptor-ligand interaction, and ends with regulation of a downstream cellular process. The pathway can start from the plasma membrane, Golgi or nuclear membrane.

ADPRHL1.functional_summary: ADPRHL1 exhibits ADP-ribosylarginine-[protein] hydrolase activity, catalyzing the removal of ADP-ribose from arginine residues on proteins, which aligns with its role in protein de-ADP-ribosylation. It is also implicated in cardiac-specific processes such as cardiac chamber ballooning and cardiac myofibril assembly, indicating a function in heart morphogenesis and muscle structure development. Localization to the sarcomere suggests that ADPRHL1 contributes to the organization or maintenance of the contractile apparatus in cardiac muscle cells.
ADPRHL1.expression_interpretation: ADPRHL1 expression is enriched in muscle-related tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in skeletal muscle and cardiac tissues such as the left ventricle and atrial appendage. Moderate expression is also detected in nerve and arterial tissues, though at notably lower levels compared to muscle. This pattern may suggest a functional role for ADPRHL1 in muscle and cardiovascular systems relative to other tissues measured.
ADPRHL1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of ADPRHL1 comprises nine interactions, highlighting associations with several partners involved in diverse cellular functions. Notably, the interactions with GRTP1 and DCUN1D2 suggest potential roles in regulatory processes, supported by generally high confidence in these connections. Overall, the network reflects a multifaceted interaction profile without clear indication of a specific pathway or complex.
ADPRHL1.gene_summary: ADPRHL1 encodes an ADP-ribosylhydrolase-like protein involved in protein de-ADP-ribosylation and cardiac myofibril assembly, playing a critical role in cardiac chamber ballooning. It shows nine protein interactions, with its top partners including GRTP1, DCUN1D2, and TMCO3. Expression of ADPRHL1 is highest in skeletal muscle. Pathogenic mutations in ADPRHL1 cause cardiac defects characterized by impaired heart chamber growth and myofibrillogenesis, and are also linked to increased prostate cancer risk, highlighting its role in both cardiac development and oncogenesis. The literature on ADPRHL1 spans themes including cardiac development and function, cancer risk and progression, and regulation of ADP-ribosylation, with recent studies investigating molecular mechanisms underlying metastasis.

AKAP17A.expression_interpretation: AKAP17A shows higher expression in several tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in ovary, spleen, and thyroid among the tissues measured. Additionally, notable expression is present in the endocervix and EBV-transformed lymphocytes, indicating enrichment in these tissue types relative to others. This pattern may suggest a role for AKAP17A in reproductive and immune-related tissues, although further investigation is required to clarify its functional significance.
AKAP17A.interaction_interpretation: [LOW_EVIDENCE] No protein interactions are recorded for AKAP17A in STRING.
AKAP17A.gene_summary: AKAP17A encodes a protein involved in the regulation of mRNA splicing and protein synthesis, notably influencing hypoxic adaptation and tumor growth through modulation of HIF1α protein levels. It has no confirmed interaction partners, with zero recorded interactions. Expression of AKAP17A is highest in the ovary and spleen. Clinically, AKAP17A is associated with altered cellular responses in cancer progression, particularly ovarian cancer sensitivity to platinum-based therapy, and its transcript levels correlate with aging phenotypes such as cognitive decline and physical deterioration. The literature on AKAP17A spans themes including RNA splicing regulation, hypoxic tumor adaptation, and ageing-associated splicing factors, with studies investigating its roles in tumor biology and neurodegenerative phenotypes.

CNP.functional_summary: CNP catalyzes the hydrolysis of nucleoside 2',3'-cyclic phosphate to nucleoside 2'-phosphate, indicating a role in the cyclic nucleotide catabolic process. It is also implicated in chemical synaptic transmission, suggesting involvement in neurotransmitter release and postsynaptic activation. Localization to the cytoplasm and mitochondrion is consistent with functions related to intracellular signaling and energy metabolism, although mechanistic detail remains limited.
CNP.expression_interpretation: CNP expression is enriched in neural tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the spinal cord (cervical c-1) relative to other measured tissues. Additional brain regions, including the substantia nigra, hippocampus, and putamen, as well as peripheral nerve tissue such as the tibial nerve, also show elevated expression compared to non-neural tissues. This pattern may suggest a role for CNP in nervous system function, although expression in other tissues measured is comparatively lower.
CNP.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network for CNP reveals a concentrated set of associations predominantly involving proteins integral to myelin structure and glial cell function. Notably, interactions with MBP, GFAP, and MAG suggest a role in oligodendrocyte biology, supported by generally high confidence in these connections. This network underscores CNP's involvement in cellular processes related to neural support and myelination.
CNP.gene_summary: CNP encodes 2',3'-cyclic nucleotide 3' phosphodiesterase, an enzyme involved in cyclic nucleotide catabolic processes and chemical synaptic transmission. It interacts with 105 partners, most notably MBP, GFAP, MAG, PLP1, and OLIG2, and is annotated to localise in the extracellular region, cytoplasm, and mitochondrion. Expression of CNP is highest in the spinal cord (cervical c-1) of the brain. CNP causes hypomyelinating leukodystrophy type 20 (HLD20), expanding the clinical spectrum of this neurological disorder characterized by defective myelination; genetic variants correlate with decreased CNP expression in patients. The literature on CNP spans themes including neurological disorders, cellular metabolism, and cardiovascular function, with studies investigating its structural features, functional roles, and potential as a therapeutic target.

COL11A1.functional_summary: COL11A1 functions as an extracellular matrix structural constituent that contributes to the structural integrity and tensile strength of the extracellular matrix. It is involved in collagen fibril organization, influencing the size and arrangement of collagen fibrils within the matrix. Localization to the extracellular region and incorporation into collagen type XI trimers suggest a role in skeletal system morphogenesis by organizing collagenous structures essential for skeletal development. Mechanistic detail beyond these functions is limited based on the provided annotations.
COL11A1.expression_interpretation: COL11A1 expression is highest within the GTEx dataset in cultured fibroblasts, with notably elevated levels compared to other tissues measured. Additionally, this gene shows enriched expression in testis, tibial nerve, hypothalamus, and pituitary relative to most other tissues. These patterns may suggest a role for COL11A1 in connective tissue and certain neural or endocrine-related tissues within the scope of the GTEx dataset.
COL11A1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of COL11A1 reveals extensive connectivity primarily with other collagen family members, indicating its integral role in extracellular matrix organization. Interactions with COL1A2 (0.992), COL5A2 (0.976), and COL2A1 (0.976) occur with high confidence, underscoring a robust association within the collagen network. This pattern suggests a coordinated involvement in structural matrix assembly without implying specific pathway participation.
COL11A1.gene_summary: COL11A1 encodes the alpha 1 chain of type XI collagen, a structural protein involved in collagen fibril organization and skeletal system morphogenesis. It interacts with 158 partners, most prominently COL1A2, COL5A2, COL2A1, COL1A1, and COL3A1, and is annotated to extracellular regions and collagen trimers. Expression of COL11A1 is highest in cultured fibroblasts. Clinically, COL11A1 is strongly associated with hearing loss and Stickler syndrome as well as cancer progression, notably pancreatic and colorectal cancers, with implications for fibrosis and chemoresistance. The literature on COL11A1 spans themes including hearing loss and Stickler syndrome, cancer progression and therapy, and extracellular matrix remodeling, with studies investigating gene regulation and epigenetics.

DHRSX.expression_interpretation: DHRSX expression is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the cervix (both endocervix and ectocervix), cultured fibroblasts, thyroid, and prostate. These tissues show notably higher expression relative to most others measured, indicating a pattern of tissue-preferential expression rather than ubiquitous distribution. This profile may suggest functional relevance of DHRSX in these tissue types, although further investigation is required to clarify its biological roles.
DHRSX.interaction_interpretation: [LOW_EVIDENCE] No protein interactions are recorded for DHRSX in STRING.
DHRSX.gene_summary: DHRSX encodes an enzyme essential for dolichol biosynthesis, catalyzing critical steps in this pathway that underpin N-glycosylation processes. It has no confidently identified protein interaction partners, with interaction data showing zero reported partners. Expression of DHRSX is highest in the cervix, specifically the endocervix. Mutations in DHRSX cause a congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by impaired dolichol synthesis and defective N-glycosylation, which impact cellular glycoprotein processing pathways. The literature on DHRSX spans themes including dolichol biosynthesis and glycosylation, X chromosome gene dosage effects, and autophagy regulation under starvation, with studies also investigating its role in neurodevelopmental disorders genetics.

F8A1.functional_summary: F8A1 is implicated in endosomal transport and vesicle cytoskeletal trafficking, indicating a role in the directed movement of substances via endosomes along cytoskeletal fibers. It also participates in protein binding and negatively regulates proteasomal protein catabolic processes, suggesting involvement in modulating protein degradation pathways. Localization to the early endosome and cytoplasm is consistent with a function in sorting and trafficking of vesicular cargo within the cell.
F8A1.expression_interpretation: [LOW_EVIDENCE] No expression data available for F8A1 in GTEx.
F8A1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of F8A1 reveals a focused set of associations primarily involving proteins related to coagulation and neuronal functions. Notably, interactions with F8 and its homologs suggest a conserved functional relationship, while the connection with HTT indicates potential links to neurobiological processes. These interactions are characterized by generally high confidence, underscoring their potential biological relevance.
F8A1.gene_summary: F8A1 encodes a protein associated with coagulation factor VIII and functions primarily in endosomal transport, vesicle cytoskeletal trafficking, and negatively regulating proteasomal protein catabolism. It engages in nine known protein interactions, with its top partners including HTT, F8, F8A2, F8A3, and ECEL1. F8A1 is annotated to both the nucleus and cytoplasm as well as the early endosome. Clinically, F8A1 is implicated in severe Hemophilia A through gene inversion events affecting its structure and is linked to type 1 diabetes risk via regulatory genetic variation on the X chromosome. The literature on F8A1 spans themes including X-chromosome genetic variation and Hemophilia A genetic mechanisms, with related broader research contexts involving neural progenitor transcriptional regulation and Mediator complex function in associated gene networks.

F8A2.functional_summary: No GO annotations are currently recorded in the Gene Ontology database for this gene. Functional characterisation cannot be determined from annotation data alone.
F8A2.expression_interpretation: [LOW_EVIDENCE] No expression data available for F8A2 in GTEx.
F8A2.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of F8A2 reveals a focused set of interactions predominantly involving proteins associated with intracellular trafficking and vesicular transport. Notably, its interactions with HTT and RAB5A suggest a role in endosomal dynamics, supported by generally high confidence scores. The presence of closely related family members F8A1 and F8A3 further indicates potential functional or regulatory relationships within this protein family.
F8A2.gene_summary: F8A2 encodes the HAP40 protein, which functions in mediating endosome movement. It engages in interactions with 10 partners, notably HTT, RAB5A, F8A1, F8A3, and HAP1. Expression data for F8A2 are not available for any specific tissue. F8A2 is implicated in severe Hemophilia A through gene inversion events involving its region, with potential variation in expression observed between populations, but no inheritance pattern is explicitly described. The literature on F8A2 includes studies on hemophilia A genetic mechanisms and gene expression variation by ancestry, with less direct evidence regarding immune response regulation; no studies specifically investigate transcriptional regulation in neural progenitor cells.

F8A3.functional_summary: No GO annotations are currently recorded in the Gene Ontology database for this gene. Functional characterisation cannot be determined from annotation data alone.
F8A3.expression_interpretation: F8A3 expression is consistently low across the tissues measured in the GTEx dataset, with little variation observed among the different tissue types. The gene shows slightly higher expression in thyroid, arterial tissues, tibial nerve, and endocervical tissues relative to others, but these differences are modest and do not indicate strong tissue specificity. Overall, this pattern suggests that F8A3 may have low overall expression or may be more prominently expressed in tissues not included in the GTEx sampling.
F8A3.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of F8A3 reveals associations with a limited set of partners, including HTT and closely related F8A family members, suggesting potential functional or evolutionary relationships within this group. The interactions include some high confidence connections with robust evidence, though overall confidence levels vary and average to a moderate confidence. This network highlights a focused interaction profile rather than broad connectivity.
F8A3.gene_summary: F8A3 is named coagulation factor VIII associated 3, suggesting a relationship to coagulation factor VIII, but direct involvement in the blood coagulation process is not established by available functional data. It interacts with six partners, including HTT, F8A1, F8A2, H2AB3, and ANKRD24. Expression of F8A3 is highest in the thyroid. Clinically, F8A3 is involved in severe Hemophilia A cases and carrier status by its role within the Factor VIII gene complex, with diagnostic assays targeting the F8A2/F8A3 flanking regions to detect relevant inversions. The literature on F8A3 spans themes including X chromosome gene regulation, Hemophilia A genetic mutations, and promoter activity in neurodevelopment, with studies investigating PCR-based genetic diagnostics.

GYG2.functional_summary: GYG2 functions as a glycosyltransferase catalyzing the transfer of glucose residues from UDP-glucose to glycogenin, initiating glycogen biosynthesis through self-glucosylation and elongation of glucosyl chains. Its activity in the glycogen biosynthetic process indicates a key role in the formation of glycogen, a branched polymer of D-glucose residues. Localization of GYG2 to the cytosol and cytoplasm is consistent with its involvement in carbohydrate metabolism within the cellular milieu. Mechanistic detail beyond these functions is limited based on the provided annotations.
GYG2.expression_interpretation: GYG2 expression is enriched in adipose tissues within the GTEx dataset, showing the highest levels in subcutaneous and visceral adipose depots relative to other measured tissues. Moderate expression is also observed in mammary tissue and certain brain regions, including the spinal cord and substantia nigra, indicating a broader but variable pattern across these tissues. This distribution may suggest tissue-specific roles in energy storage or neural function, although further investigation is required to clarify these potential associations.
GYG2.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of GYG2 reveals a focused set of interactions predominantly with key glycogen metabolism-related proteins, including GYS1, GYS2, and GYG1, suggesting a central role in glycogen biosynthesis regulation. These interactions occur with generally high confidence, underscoring the functional relevance of GYG2 within this metabolic context. Additional partners such as GBE1 and AGL further support its involvement in glycogen processing.
GYG2.gene_summary: GYG2 encodes glycogenin 2, an enzyme that initiates glycogen biosynthesis by self-glucosylation to prime glycogen chains. It coordinates with 69 interaction partners, most notably glycogen synthases GYS1 and GYS2, glycogenin 1 (GYG1), 1,4-alpha-glucan branching enzyme (GBE1), and amylo-alpha-1,6-glucosidase (AGL); the protein localizes to the nucleus, cytoplasm, and cytosol. Expression of GYG2 is highest in subcutaneous adipose tissue. Clinically, GYG2 has been implicated in regulating glucose homeostasis and glycogen metabolism, with associations reported in cancer contexts such as glioma, where its expression relates to tumor growth and microenvironment features, and it also emerges as a biomarker linking mitochondrial function to aging processes in adipose tissue; these findings underline a phenotypic spectrum including metabolic and proliferative disorders. The literature on GYG2 spans themes including glycogen metabolism regulation, cancer biology, mitochondrial function and aging, with recent investigations focusing on its role in metabolic homeostasis and tumorigenesis.

HSD17B7P2 has limited dedicated literature; it appears incidentally in studies concerning neurodevelopmental disorders, transcriptional regulation, mediator complex function, genetic association analyses, and neural progenitor cell biology, but no publications focus specifically on this gene. The literature on HSD17B7P2 spans themes including neurodevelopment, transcriptional regulation, and genetics, with recent investigations centering on neuroimaging phenotypes related to neurodegenerative conditions.

LINC00839.functional_summary: [LOW_EVIDENCE] Insufficient annotation data to generate experimental relevance context for LINC00839.
LINC00839.expression_interpretation: LINC00839 shows higher expression in kidney cortex relative to other tissues measured within the GTEx dataset, with notable enrichment also observed in spleen and several brain regions including the caudate, frontal cortex, and nucleus accumbens. This pattern suggests that LINC00839 may have functional relevance in both renal and specific neural tissues. The expression profile does not indicate exclusive tissue specificity but rather a tendency toward elevated levels in these particular tissues among those assessed.

LINC00839.gene_summary: LINC00839 encodes a long intergenic non-protein coding RNA involved in regulatory functions at the RNA level. It has no reported direct protein interaction partners, with zero interactions identified in available datasets. Expression of LINC00839 is highest in the kidney cortex. Clinically, LINC00839 is strongly associated with various carcinomas, including lung adenocarcinoma, oral squamous cell carcinoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, where it promotes tumor progression, metastasis, and correlates with clinicopathological features and diagnostic value. The literature on LINC00839 spans themes including cancer progression mechanisms, lncRNA-miRNA interactions, and signaling pathway activation, with current studies investigating its role in transcriptional regulation and therapy resistance.

LINC02688.functional_summary: [LOW_EVIDENCE] Insufficient annotation data to generate experimental relevance context for LINC02688.
LINC02688.expression_interpretation: LINC02688 shows the highest expression within the GTEx dataset in the spleen, with notably lower levels observed in brain regions such as the nucleus accumbens and cerebellum, as well as in testis and the terminal ileum of the small intestine. This pattern indicates that LINC02688 is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, particularly the spleen, relative to others measured. The elevated expression in the spleen may suggest a potential role related to immune or hematopoietic functions, although further investigation is required to clarify its biological significance.

LINC02688.gene_summary: LINC02688 encodes a long intergenic non-protein coding RNA without assigned biological processes or molecular functions. It has no reported protein interaction partners, reflecting a total of zero identified interactions. Expression of LINC02688 is highest in the spleen. Clinically, LINC02688 has been incorporated as a necroptosis-related long non-coding RNA in prognostic risk models for cervical squamous cell carcinoma and endocervical adenocarcinoma, suggesting its relevance in cancer prognosis and immune response regulation. The literature on LINC02688 has been studied in the context of lncRNA involvement in cancer prognosis, immune response modulation, and necroptosis mechanisms.

MED12.functional_summary: MED12 functions as a transcription coregulator that modulates the transcription of specific gene sets by interacting with DNA-binding transcription factors, often altering chromatin structure or facilitating transcriptional activation. It exhibits sequence-specific DNA binding to RNA polymerase II cis-regulatory regions and positively regulates transcription initiation by RNA polymerase II. Localization of MED12 to the nucleus and nucleoplasm is consistent with its role in regulating gene expression at the chromatin level.
MED12.expression_interpretation: MED12 shows higher expression in reproductive tissues such as the ovary, uterus, and cervix (both endocervix and ectocervix) relative to other tissues measured within the GTEx dataset. Additionally, nerve tissue from the tibial region also exhibits elevated expression levels among the tissues assessed. This pattern may suggest a functional relevance of MED12 in these specific tissue types within the context of the GTEx data.
MED12.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of MED12 reveals extensive connectivity, with 183 identified interactions highlighting its central role in cellular processes. Notably, MED12 interacts strongly with MED13, MED6, and MED24, suggesting a tightly associated functional module. These interactions are supported with generally high confidence, underscoring the robustness of the network data.
MED12.gene_summary: MED12 encodes a key subunit of the Mediator complex responsible for regulating transcription by RNA polymerase II. It engages with a network of 183 interaction partners, most notably MED13, MED6, MED24, CCNC, and MED22, and is annotated to the nucleoplasm. Expression of MED12 is highest in the ovary. MED12 causes a spectrum of developmental disorders including X-linked intellectual disability syndromes such as Lujan-Fryns syndrome and Hardikar syndrome, which can feature congenital diaphragmatic hernia and variable neurodevelopmental impairment. The literature on MED12 spans themes including intellectual disability linked to MED12 mutations, Mediator complex transcription regulation, and the broader phenotypic spectrum of MED12-related developmental disorders, with studies investigating variant effects on transcriptional control and chromatin modification.

NDST4.functional_summary: NDST4 exhibits sulfotransferase activity, specifically catalyzing the transfer of sulfate groups to the amino groups of heparan sulfate chains, thereby contributing to the biosynthesis of heparan sulfate proteoglycans. This enzymatic function involves the modification of alpha-D-glucosaminyl residues within heparan sulfate, facilitating the formation of sulfated glycosaminoglycan structures. Localization to the Golgi apparatus and its membrane suggests that NDST4 functions in the post-translational modification and processing of proteoglycans within the secretory pathway.
NDST4.expression_interpretation: NDST4 expression is generally low across the tissues measured in the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in nerve (tibial), prostate, ovary, and testis among the tissues measured. Moderate expression is also noted in the spleen relative to other tissues. This pattern suggests that NDST4 may have a role in these specific tissues, although its overall low expression across the dataset may indicate additional expression in tissues not captured by GTEx or a generally low abundance.
NDST4.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of NDST4 encompasses 39 interactions, prominently featuring partners involved in heparan sulfate biosynthesis and modification. Notably, interactions with HS2ST1 and several glypicans suggest a role in extracellular matrix remodeling. These associations are supported with moderate confidence, underscoring NDST4's functional relevance in glycosaminoglycan metabolism.
NDST4.gene_summary: NDST4 encodes an enzyme with N-sulfotransferase activity involved in the biosynthesis of heparan sulfate proteoglycans. It coordinates with 39 partners, most notably HS2ST1, GLCE, and glypicans GPC5, GPC3, and GPC2. Expression of NDST4 is highest in nerve tissue, specifically in the tibial nerve. NDST4 has been identified as a candidate tumor suppressor gene with downregulation and allelic loss linked to colorectal cancer, where its altered function affects colonic epithelial cell differentiation and predicts adverse prognosis. The literature on NDST4 spans themes including heparan sulfate biosynthesis, cancer tumor suppression, and enzyme isoform characterization, with recent studies investigating its role in colonic epithelial differentiation.

PCDHA3.functional_summary: PCDHA3 functions in calcium ion binding and interacts with cell adhesion molecules, facilitating cell adhesion processes including homophilic cell-cell adhesion. These activities contribute to nervous system development by promoting the attachment of cells to one another. Localization to the plasma membrane and membrane compartments is consistent with a role in mediating cell-cell interactions at the cell surface.
PCDHA3.expression_interpretation: PCDHA3 shows higher expression in testis relative to other tissues measured within the GTEx dataset, with notable expression also observed in brain regions including the cerebellum and cerebellar hemisphere. Additionally, reproductive tissues such as the uterus and ovary exhibit elevated levels compared to most other tissues. This pattern suggests that PCDHA3 expression is enriched in specific neural and reproductive tissues within the GTEx dataset.
PCDHA3.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of PCDHA3 reveals a focused set of interactions predominantly with other protocadherin alpha family members, suggesting a role in homophilic or closely related heterophilic interactions. These associations are supported with generally high confidence, indicating robust evidence for their biological relevance. This pattern underscores the potential importance of PCDHA3 in mediating cell-cell adhesion processes within neural contexts.
PCDHA3.gene_summary: PCDHA3 encodes protocadherin alpha 3, a member of the cadherin superfamily involved in mediating cell-cell adhesion important for nervous system development. It has nine known interactions, notably with other protocadherin alpha cluster members including PCDHA6, PCDHA1, and PCDHA2. PCDHA3 is expressed most highly in the testis and brain’s cerebellum. Clinically, PCDHA3 is implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia, where mutations disrupt synaptic adhesion; it also has associations with cancer metastasis inhibition and a dental phenotype known as short root anomaly. The literature on PCDHA3 spans themes including neuropsychiatric disorder genetics, cancer metastasis inhibition, and protocadherin gene cluster variation, with studies investigating its role in epithelial-mesenchymal transition and gene regulation by noncoding RNA.

PCDHA6.functional_summary: PCDHA6 functions in cell adhesion by mediating the attachment of a cell to another cell or to an underlying substrate through homophilic interactions with identical adhesion molecules. It binds calcium ions, which may regulate its adhesive properties. Localization to the plasma membrane and extracellular region is consistent with a role in facilitating cell-cell contacts during nervous system development. Mechanistic detail beyond these interactions is limited based on the available annotations.
PCDHA6.expression_interpretation: PCDHA6 expression is enriched in specific brain regions within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the cerebellar hemisphere and cerebellum. Moderate expression is also detected in the pituitary, frontal cortex, and spinal cord relative to other tissues measured. This pattern may suggest a role for PCDHA6 in neural tissues, although expression in other unmeasured tissues cannot be excluded.
PCDHA6.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of PCDHA6 reveals a limited number of interactions predominantly with other protocadherin alpha family members, suggesting a role in homophilic or closely related heterophilic associations. These interactions are characterized by generally high confidence, underscoring the specificity and potential functional relevance within this subgroup of cell adhesion molecules.
PCDHA6.gene_summary: PCDHA6 encodes protocadherin alpha 6, a protein that mediates cell adhesion and is involved in nervous system development. It interacts with five partners, most notably PCDHA3, PCDHA10, PCDHA7, PCDHA2, and PCDHA8. PCDHA6 expression is highest in the brain, specifically in the cerebellar hemisphere and cerebellum. Variants in PCDHA6 have been linked to short root anomaly, a dental phenotype, and decreased expression of PCDHA6 has been observed in neurons with mutations in DISC1 associated with psychiatric illness, suggesting involvement in neural development and neurite growth impairment. The literature on PCDHA6 spans themes including protocadherin gene variants, neurite growth regulation, and gene expression modulation, with studies investigating its role in neural progenitor cell function.

PCDHB5.functional_summary: PCDHB5 functions in calcium ion binding and protein binding, including interactions with cell adhesion molecules, which supports its role in mediating cell adhesion through homophilic cell-cell adhesion mechanisms. It is involved in biological processes such as synapse assembly and chemical synaptic transmission, indicating a role in the formation and function of synaptic connections. Localization to the plasma membrane and synapse is consistent with a role in nervous system development and the establishment of neuronal connectivity. Mechanistic detail is limited by the available annotations.
PCDHB5.expression_interpretation: PCDHB5 shows higher expression in reproductive tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the ovary, testis, uterus, and cervix among the highest-expressing tissues measured. Additionally, notable expression is observed in the pituitary relative to other tissues. This pattern may suggest a role for PCDHB5 in reproductive and endocrine-related functions, although further investigation is required to clarify its biological significance.
PCDHB5.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of PCDHB5 reveals a focused set of associations predominantly with other protocadherin family members, suggesting a role in cell-cell adhesion or signaling within neural contexts. Notably, interactions with PCDHB2, PCDHB11, and PCDHB3 indicate a conserved functional relationship among clustered protocadherins. Additionally, the connection to MYLK3 may reflect a broader regulatory interface, although this interaction warrants further investigation to clarify its biological significance.
PCDHB5.gene_summary: PCDHB5 encodes a protocadherin protein involved in cell adhesion, homophilic cell-cell adhesion, chemical synaptic transmission, nervous system development, and synapse assembly. It has 19 known interacting partners, most notably PCDHB2, MYLK3, PCDHB11, PCDHB3, and PCDHB6. Expression of PCDHB5 is highest in the ovary and testis. Clinically, PCDHB5 has been implicated in oncogenic processes, particularly in gastric cancer where its upregulation correlates with poor prognosis and immune infiltration; it is also noted within gene networks linked to retinoblastoma progression and epigenetically regulated in renal cell carcinoma metastasis. The literature on PCDHB5 spans themes including its oncogenic role in cancer, immune infiltration in tumors, and transcriptional regulation mechanisms, with recent studies investigating its expression regulation and functional impact in tumor biology.

PREX1.functional_summary: PREX1 functions as a guanyl-nucleotide exchange factor that stimulates the exchange of GDP for GTP on signaling GTPases, thereby activating them. It is involved in the positive regulation of cell migration and modulates actin filament polymerization, processes essential for cellular motility. Localization to the plasma membrane and cytosol suggests a role in transducing signals from membrane-associated receptors to cytoskeletal dynamics. Mechanistic detail beyond these activities is limited based on the provided annotations.
PREX1.expression_interpretation: PREX1 shows higher expression in whole blood relative to other tissues measured within the GTEx dataset, with notably elevated levels also observed in the spinal cord, spleen, EBV-transformed lymphocytes, and lung. This pattern suggests that PREX1 expression is enriched in several hematopoietic and immune-related tissues, as well as certain neural and pulmonary tissues. These observations may suggest a role for PREX1 in functions associated with these tissue types, although further investigation is needed to clarify its specific biological relevance.
PREX1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of PREX1 encompasses 66 interactions, prominently featuring small GTPases such as RAC1, RAC3, and CDC42, which suggests a role in regulating cytoskeletal dynamics. Interactions with G-protein subunits GNB1 and GNG2 further indicate involvement in signal transduction processes. These associations are supported with generally high confidence, underscoring the functional relevance of PREX1 within these molecular contexts.
PREX1.gene_summary: PREX1 encodes a phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate dependent Rac exchange factor 1, regulating signaling pathways related to actin filament polymerization and cell migration. It coordinates with 66 interaction partners, with top partners including RAC3, RAC1, GNB1, CDC42, and GNG2. Expression of PREX1 is highest in whole blood. While the provided literature associates PREX1 primarily with cancer progression mechanisms, immune cell regulation, and metabolic regulation, direct causative links to specific inherited diseases or phenotypic syndromes are not established. The literature on PREX1 spans themes including cancer progression mechanisms, immune cell regulation, and signal transduction pathways, with recent studies investigating protein structural dynamics.

PROKR1.functional_summary: PROKR1 functions as a G protein-coupled receptor that binds extracellular ligands, such as neuropeptides, to initiate intracellular signaling by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP on the alpha subunit of heterotrimeric G-proteins. This activity triggers downstream cellular responses, including those involved in neuropeptide signaling pathways and hormone stimulus responses. Localization of PROKR1 to the plasma membrane is consistent with its role in transducing extracellular signals into intracellular effects. Mechanistic detail beyond these signaling events is limited based on the provided annotations.
PROKR1.expression_interpretation: PROKR1 expression is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the pituitary, followed by testis and visceral adipose tissue. Moderate expression is also detected in breast mammary tissue and the sigmoid colon, while other tissues show comparatively lower levels. This pattern may suggest a role for PROKR1 in endocrine and reproductive tissues, although expression in additional tissues not captured by GTEx cannot be excluded.
PROKR1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of PROKR1 encompasses 82 interactions, prominently featuring ligands PROK1 and PROK2, which underscores its role in ligand-receptor dynamics. Additional interactions with proteins such as ADCY3 and MRAP2 suggest involvement in signal transduction processes, with several interactions supported by generally high confidence. This network highlights PROKR1's functional connectivity within cellular signaling contexts without implying specific pathway affiliations.
PROKR1.gene_summary: PROKR1 encodes prokineticin receptor 1, a G protein-coupled receptor involved in mediating neuropeptide signaling and regulating circadian rhythm and cellular responses to hormone stimuli. It has 82 known interactions, with key partners including PROK1, PROK2, ADCY3, MRAP2, and ALDH18A1. PROKR1 expression is highest in the pituitary. Clinically, PROKR1 has been studied in contexts related to reproductive biology, energy metabolism, angiogenesis, vascular function, muscle function, and regeneration, although no definitive disease-causing mutations are described in the current literature. The literature on PROKR1 spans themes including reproductive biology regulation, energy metabolism control, and angiogenesis and vascular function, with recent studies investigating its role in muscle function and regeneration.

PUDP.functional_summary: PUDP exhibits phosphatase activity, specifically catalyzing the hydrolysis of pseudouridine 5'-phosphate to pseudouridine and phosphate, indicating a role in nucleotide metabolism. Its ability to bind proteins suggests potential regulatory interactions or complex formation. Localization to the cytosol is consistent with a function in cytoplasmic nucleotide processing or turnover. Mechanistic detail beyond these activities is limited based on the available annotations.
PUDP.expression_interpretation: PUDP expression is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in EBV-transformed lymphocytes, followed by cultured fibroblasts and skeletal muscle. Moderate expression is also noted in vaginal and tibial nerve tissues relative to other measured tissues. This pattern may suggest a role for PUDP in cell types related to immune function, connective tissue, and muscle, although further investigation is needed to clarify its biological significance.
PUDP.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of PUDP encompasses 88 partners, with prominent associations including PGGHG, GPI, and AGXT. These interactions suggest a functional linkage to proteins involved in metabolic processes, supported by generally high confidence scores for several key partners. The network topology indicates PUDP's potential role in diverse cellular contexts without strong evidence for specific pathway or complex membership.
PUDP.gene_summary: PUDP encodes a pseudouridine 5'-phosphatase enzyme that catalyzes the dephosphorylation of pseudouridine-5'-phosphate. It has 88 known protein interactions, with the most prominent partners being PGGHG, GPI, AGXT, YIPF6, and STS. PUDP expression is highest in EBV-transformed lymphocytes. Clinically, PUDP is located within an X chromosome region associated with deletions causing X-linked ichthyosis, although direct causative roles for PUDP itself have not been established in these disorders. The literature on PUDP spans themes including X chromosome genetic variation, pseudouridine metabolism, and neurodevelopmental disorders, with studies investigating transcriptional regulation in neural progenitor cells.

RGPD1.functional_summary: RGPD1 is implicated in the transfer of SUMO groups between proteins, catalyzing the covalent attachment of SUMO from one protein to another. It is associated with processes involving the movement of proteins bearing nuclear localization signals into the nucleus as well as the export of substances from the nucleus, indicating a role in nucleocytoplasmic transport. Localization to the nuclear pore complex suggests that RGPD1 may facilitate or regulate transport across the nuclear envelope, although mechanistic details remain limited.
RGPD1.expression_interpretation: RGPD1 expression is highest within the GTEx dataset in testis, showing notably greater levels compared to other tissues measured. Moderate expression is observed in the pituitary and liver, while expression in cervix endocervix and brain cerebellum is comparatively lower. This pattern suggests that RGPD1 may have tissue-enriched roles in testis and possibly endocrine-related tissues, although expression in other tissues is generally low within the dataset.
RGPD1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of RGPD1 encompasses 43 interactions, prominently featuring partners involved in nucleocytoplasmic transport and Ran GTPase regulation, such as RAN, RANGAP1, and RCC1. The presence of GRIP1 and NPIPB6 suggests additional functional associations, with several interactions supported by generally high confidence. This network highlights RGPD1's potential role in processes related to nuclear transport dynamics.
RGPD1.gene_summary: RGPD1 encodes a protein involved in the import and export of nuclear localization signal-bearing proteins, contributing to nucleocytoplasmic transport. It coordinates with 43 interaction partners, most notably GRIP1, RAN, RANGAP1, and RCC1. Expression of RGPD1 is highest in the testis. There are no established clinical conditions or inheritance patterns directly attributed to RGPD1 based on current literature or disease associations. RGPD1 has limited dedicated literature. It has appeared as an incidental finding across studies of epigenetic regulation, immune response modulation, genetic variant analysis, telomere biology, and transcriptional regulation in neural progenitor cells, but no papers in this set focus specifically on RGPD1.

SNRPN.functional_summary: SNRPN functions in RNA binding and protein binding, specifically interacting with small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles. It participates in mRNA splicing via the spliceosome, facilitating the excision of introns and joining of exons to produce mature mRNA transcripts. Localization of SNRPN to the nucleoplasm and spliceosomal complex is consistent with a role in RNA processing within the nucleus. Mechanistic detail beyond these interactions is limited based on the provided annotations.
SNRPN.expression_interpretation: SNRPN shows higher expression in several brain regions within the GTEx dataset, with the cerebellar hemisphere, frontal cortex, cerebellum, and cortex among the highest-expressing tissues measured. Additionally, the pituitary exhibits elevated expression relative to most other tissues, indicating enrichment in specific neural and neuroendocrine tissues. This pattern may suggest a role for SNRPN in brain-related functions, although expression in other tissues measured is comparatively lower.
SNRPN.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of SNRPN reveals extensive connectivity, with a total of 248 interactions predominantly involving small nuclear ribonucleoprotein components. The top partners, including SNRPD3, SNRPF, and SNRPD1, suggest a focused interaction profile consistent with roles in RNA processing. These interactions are characterized by generally high confidence, underscoring the robustness of the network associations.
SNRPN.gene_summary: SNRPN encodes the small nuclear ribonucleoprotein polypeptide N, which functions primarily in mRNA splicing via the spliceosome. It has 248 known interaction partners, notably including SNRPD3, SNRPF, SNRPD1, SNRPD2, and SNRPG. Expression of SNRPN is highest in the brain, particularly in the cerebellar hemisphere. SNRPN causes neurodevelopmental defects through abnormal methylation and imprinting alterations, as seen in Prader-Willi syndrome, manifesting in impaired neuronal differentiation, reduced neural stem cell populations, and disrupted cortical and spine development. The literature on SNRPN spans themes including imprinting and epigenetic regulation, neurodevelopment and neuronal function, and alternative splicing mechanisms, with recent studies investigating its role in rescuing neurodevelopmental impairment via regulatory interactions.

STS.functional_summary: STS encodes an enzyme with arylsulfatase and steryl-sulfatase activities, catalyzing the hydrolysis of sulfate esters from phenol sulfates and steroid sulfates, respectively, thereby contributing to the breakdown of steroids. Its sulfuric ester hydrolase activity further supports a role in cleaving sulfuric ester bonds. Localization to lysosomes and endosomes is consistent with a function in intracellular degradation and processing of sulfated molecules, while presence in the endoplasmic reticulum suggests involvement in protein maturation or trafficking. Mechanistic detail is limited to these catalytic activities and subcellular localizations.
STS.expression_interpretation: STS expression is enriched in vascular and connective tissues within the GTEx dataset, showing the highest levels in arterial tissues such as the tibial and coronary arteries. Additionally, cultured fibroblasts and EBV-transformed lymphocytes exhibit relatively elevated expression compared to most other measured tissues. This pattern may suggest a functional role for STS in vascular and connective tissue contexts, although expression in tissues not captured by GTEx cannot be excluded.
STS.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network for STS reveals a focused set of interactions primarily involving enzymes associated with steroid metabolism. These interactions occur with generally high confidence, underscoring the functional relevance of STS within this biochemical context. The network highlights STS's role in modulating steroidogenic processes through its association with key enzymatic partners.
STS.gene_summary: STS encodes steroid sulfatase, an enzyme essential for the catabolic process of steroid sulfates and involved in epidermis development. It interacts with 122 partners, notably including HSD3B1, AKR1C3, CYP17A1, HSD3B2, and SULT2B1, and is annotated to lysosome, endosome, and endoplasmic reticulum compartments. Expression of STS is highest in the artery tibial tissue. STS causes X-linked ichthyosis, a disorder characterized by scaling skin and often accompanied by neurological symptoms, with pathogenic deletions and mutations on Xp22.31 driving a broad phenotypic spectrum including contiguous gene syndromes. The literature on STS spans themes including X-linked ichthyosis genetics, neural precursor cell apoptosis, and steroid sulfatase inhibition, with studies investigating chromosomal variations and neurodevelopmental disorder mechanisms.

TCF7L2.functional_summary: TCF7L2 functions as a DNA-binding transcription factor that modulates transcription mediated by RNA polymerase II through sequence-specific binding to cis-regulatory regions, including transcription factor recognition sequences. It is involved in both the regulation and negative regulation of transcription, potentially acting as a transcriptional repressor by interacting with transcription corepressors. Localization of TCF7L2 to the nucleus and chromatin is consistent with its role in directly influencing gene expression at the level of chromosomal DNA.
TCF7L2.expression_interpretation: TCF7L2 expression is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in artery (tibial), uterus, subcutaneous adipose tissue, ectocervix, and mammary tissue. These tissues show notably higher expression relative to others measured, indicating a pattern of tissue-specific enrichment rather than uniform expression. The observed distribution may suggest roles for TCF7L2 in vascular, reproductive, and adipose-related functions within the sampled tissues.
TCF7L2.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of TCF7L2 encompasses 247 interactions, prominently featuring partners such as CTNNB1, NLK, and CTBP1, which suggests a central role in transcriptional regulation. These interactions include several with very high confidence, indicating robust experimental support for key partners, alongside others with moderate confidence. The presence of key co-regulators like BCL9 and EP300 further underscores TCF7L2's involvement in modulating gene expression dynamics.
TCF7L2.gene_summary: TCF7L2 encodes a transcription factor that plays a critical role in regulating transcription by RNA polymerase II, as well as in blood vessel development and gluconeogenesis. It has 247 known interaction partners, with the top partners including CTNNB1, NLK, CTBP1, BCL9, and EP300; TCF7L2 is annotated to chromatin, nucleus, and nucleoplasm. Expression of TCF7L2 is highest in artery tissue, specifically the tibial artery. Variations in TCF7L2 are causative for diverse conditions including neurodevelopmental disorders and cancers, where it influences pathways involved in disease progression and therapy response; clinical phenotypes linked to TCF7L2 involve tumor heterogeneity and metabolic regulation, with a notable role in modulating tumor-associated macrophage differentiation and colorectal cancer progression. The literature on TCF7L2 spans themes including Wnt/β-catenin signaling, neurodevelopmental disorders, and cancer progression and therapy, with studies investigating its role in metabolic regulation.

TMEM163.functional_summary: TMEM163 functions in zinc ion binding and participates in the transmembrane transport of zinc ions, including their import into synaptic vesicles and export across the plasma membrane, contributing to intracellular zinc ion homeostasis. It is also associated with the biological process of myelination, indicating a potential role in maintaining neuronal function. Localization of TMEM163 to lysosomes, lysosomal membranes, and late endosomes suggests involvement in zinc ion regulation within endocytic and degradative compartments, although mechanistic details remain limited.
TMEM163.expression_interpretation: TMEM163 expression is enriched in specific brain regions within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the cerebellar hemisphere and cerebellum. Additional notable expression occurs in the pituitary, spinal cord (cervical c-1), and frontal cortex (BA9), indicating a pattern of elevated expression in central nervous system tissues relative to others measured. This distribution may suggest a role for TMEM163 in neural or neuroendocrine functions, although further investigation is required to clarify its biological significance.
TMEM163.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of TMEM163 comprises a limited set of partners, indicating a potentially specialized functional role. Notably, interactions with proteins such as ACMSD and TMEM175 suggest involvement in processes related to cellular metabolism and membrane transport. These associations are supported with moderate confidence, underscoring their potential biological relevance.
TMEM163.gene_summary: TMEM163 encodes a transmembrane protein primarily involved in regulating intracellular zinc ion homeostasis, including zinc ion transmembrane transport and zinc ion import into synaptic vesicles. It interacts with six identified partners, most notably ACMSD, TMEM175, and CCDC62. Expression of TMEM163 is highest in the brain, specifically in the cerebellar hemisphere and cerebellum. Variants in TMEM163 cause a hypomyelinating leukodystrophy characterized by impaired zinc efflux, oligodendroglial dysfunction, and reduced myelin gene expression, leading to neurological deficits; TMEM163 deficiency also disrupts platelet dense granule biogenesis, implicating it in lysosome-related organelle function. The literature on TMEM163 spans themes including zinc transport and homeostasis, neurological disorders and hypomyelination, and metabolic disease associations, with recent studies investigating its role in protein interactions and cellular signalling.

TRIM61.functional_summary: TRIM61 functions as a zinc ion-binding protein with ubiquitin protein ligase activity, catalyzing the transfer of ubiquitin to substrate proteins. It is involved in the regulation of gene expression and participates in the innate immune response, indicating a role in modulating cellular defense mechanisms. Localization to the cytoplasm suggests that TRIM61 exerts its regulatory functions within the cellular milieu where protein ubiquitination and immune signaling occur.
TRIM61.expression_interpretation: TRIM61 expression is highest within the GTEx dataset in testis, showing markedly greater levels compared to other tissues measured. Moderate expression is observed in EBV-transformed lymphocytes, adrenal gland, thyroid, and pituitary, while other tissues exhibit relatively low expression. This pattern suggests that TRIM61 may have tissue-enriched roles, particularly in testis, although expression in additional tissues not captured by GTEx cannot be excluded.
TRIM61.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of TRIM61 is limited, comprising three primary partners, including ZNF558 and ZNF701, which are zinc finger proteins suggesting a potential role in transcriptional regulation. The interactions are characterized by moderate confidence, indicating reasonably reliable associations. However, the sparse network precludes definitive conclusions regarding specific functional pathways.
TRIM61.gene_summary: TRIM61 encodes a protein containing a tripartite motif that functions in the regulation of gene expression and innate immune response. It interacts with three known partners, most notably ZNF558, ZNF701, and ALG1L. Expression of TRIM61 is highest in the testis. Clinically, TRIM61 has been linked to epigenetic regulation influencing age at menarche and has associations with survival outcomes in lung squamous cell carcinoma, indicating potential roles in reproductive timing and cancer prognosis. The literature on TRIM61 spans themes including genetic regulation mechanisms, epigenetic modifications, and protein processing pathways, with recent studies investigating transcriptional regulation in neural progenitor cells.

UVRAG.functional_summary: UVRAG is implicated in autophagy, a cellular catabolic process that degrades cellular materials and non-self components, and in retrograde vesicle-mediated transport from the Golgi to the endoplasmic reticulum, which involves the directed movement of substances via coated vesicles. Its molecular functions include binding to SNARE proteins and SH3 domains, suggesting a role in protein-protein interactions critical for vesicle trafficking and membrane dynamics. Localization to the autophagosome membrane and lytic vacuole is consistent with a role in vesicle-mediated degradation and intracellular recycling processes. Mechanistic detail beyond these functions is limited based on the available GO term definitions.

UVRAG has been implicated in cancer biology, particularly through its role in autophagy regulation and tumor suppression, as well as in pigmentation disorders related to melanosome biogenesis, influencing melanoma predisposition. The literature on UVRAG spans themes including autophagy regulation, cancer biology, and protein ubiquitination, with recent studies investigating its role in microRNA-mediated control and developmental signaling.

ZDBF2.gene_summary: ZDBF2 encodes a zinc finger DBF-type containing protein involved primarily in the biological process of genomic imprinting. Clinically, ZDBF2 mutations cause disorders such as Nasopalpebral Lipoma-coloboma syndrome, with evidence indicating pathogenicity from de novo heterozygous variants; it is also implicated in modulating cancer cell behaviors, including inhibition of ferroptosis and therapy resistance in oral squamous cell carcinoma. The literature on ZDBF2 spans themes including genomic imprinting regulation, epigenetic modification mechanisms, and cancer progression and therapy resistance, with recent studies investigating the roles of its circular RNA forms in transcriptional regulation and tumor biology.

ZFP3.gene_summary: ZFP3 encodes a zinc finger protein involved in the regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II. It has eight known protein interactions, with prominent partners including RCVRN, PTGER1, POLR2L, TP53, and SPARC, and is annotated to localize in the nucleus. Expression of ZFP3 is highest in the cerebellar hemisphere and cerebellum of the brain. Studies have identified ZFP3 as part of gene signatures relevant to cancer prognosis, including lung adenocarcinoma, osteosarcoma subtype classification, and oral squamous cell carcinoma, indicating its potential as a biomarker rather than a direct causative agent of disease. ZFP3 has been studied in the context of zinc finger protein genetics, chromosomal gene localization, transcriptional regulation in neural progenitor cells, Mediator complex function, and neurodevelopmental disorder mechanisms, with current research focusing on its role in transcriptional regulation and disease associations.

ZNF558.gene_summary: ZNF558 encodes a zinc finger protein that functions as a transcriptional regulator involved in the control of DNA-templated transcription and transcription by RNA polymerase II. It engages with twelve protein partners, notably TRIM61, OR2Z1, TRIM28, MBD3L1, and SPATA18, highlighting its integration within gene regulatory networks. Expression of ZNF558 is highest in the uterus. Clinically, ZNF558 has been linked to neuronal development and psychiatric disorder genetics, with altered expression observed in neuronal cells impacting mitophagy and mitochondrial homeostasis; it is also implicated as a fusion partner in certain sarcomas. The literature on ZNF558 spans themes including gene regulatory networks, neuronal development, and structural genomic variation, with studies investigating its role in psychiatric disorder genetics.

These interactions suggest a functional linkage to proteins involved in metabolic processes, supported by generally high confidence scores for several key partners. The network topology indicates PUDP's potential role in diverse cellular contexts without strong evidence for specific pathway or complex membership.

NDST4.functional_summary: NDST4 exhibits sulfotransferase activity, specifically catalyzing the transfer of sulfate groups to the amino groups of heparan sulfate chains, thereby contributing to the biosynthesis of heparan sulfate proteoglycans. This enzymatic function involves the modification of alpha-D-glucosaminyl residues within heparan sulfate, facilitating the formation of sulfated glycosaminoglycan structures. Localization to the Golgi apparatus and its membrane suggests that NDST4 functions in the post-translational modification and processing of proteoglycans within the secretory pathway.
NDST4.expression_interpretation: NDST4 expression is generally low across the tissues measured in the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in nerve (tibial), prostate, ovary, and testis among the tissues measured. Moderate expression is also noted in the spleen relative to other tissues. This pattern suggests that NDST4 may have a role in these specific tissues, although its overall low expression across the dataset may indicate additional expression in tissues not captured by GTEx or a generally low abundance.
NDST4.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of NDST4 encompasses 39 interactions, prominently featuring partners involved in heparan sulfate biosynthesis and modification. Notably, interactions with HS2ST1 and several glypicans suggest a role in extracellular matrix remodeling. These associations are supported with generally high confidence, underscoring NDST4's functional relevance in glycosaminoglycan metabolism.

DHRSX.functional_summary: [LOW_EVIDENCE] Insufficient annotation data to generate experimental relevance context for DHRSX.
DHRSX.expression_interpretation: DHRSX expression is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the cervix (both endocervix and ectocervix), cultured fibroblasts, thyroid, and prostate. These tissues show notably higher expression relative to most others measured, indicating a pattern of tissue-preferential expression rather than ubiquitous distribution. This profile may suggest functional relevance of DHRSX in these tissue types, although further investigation is required to clarify its biological roles.
DHRSX.interaction_interpretation: [LOW_EVIDENCE] No protein interactions are recorded for DHRSX in STRING.

STS.functional_summary: STS encodes an enzyme with arylsulfatase and steryl-sulfatase activities, catalyzing the hydrolysis of sulfate esters from phenol sulfates and steroid sulfates, respectively, thereby contributing to the breakdown of steroids. Its sulfuric ester hydrolase activity further supports a role in cleaving sulfuric ester bonds. Localization to lysosomes and endosomes is consistent with a function in intracellular degradation and processing of sulfated molecules, while presence in the endoplasmic reticulum suggests involvement in protein maturation or trafficking. Mechanistic detail is limited to these catalytic activities and subcellular localizations.
STS.expression_interpretation: STS expression is enriched in vascular and connective tissues within the GTEx dataset, showing the highest levels in arterial tissues such as the tibial and coronary arteries. Additionally, cultured fibroblasts and EBV-transformed lymphocytes exhibit relatively elevated expression compared to most other measured tissues. This pattern may suggest a functional role for STS in vascular and connective tissue contexts, although expression in tissues not captured by GTEx cannot be excluded.
STS.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network for STS reveals a focused set of interactions primarily involving enzymes associated with steroid metabolism. These interactions occur with generally high confidence, underscoring the functional relevance of STS within this biochemical context. The network highlights STS's role in modulating steroidogenic processes through its association with key enzymatic partners.

biological_processes.name: negative regulation of proteasomal protein catabolic process

F8A1.functional_summary: F8A1 is implicated in endosomal transport and vesicle cytoskeletal trafficking, indicating a role in the directed movement of substances via endosomes along cytoskeletal fibers. It also participates in protein binding and negatively regulates proteasomal protein catabolic processes, suggesting involvement in modulating protein degradation pathways. Localization to the early endosome and cytoplasm is consistent with a function in sorting and trafficking of vesicular cargo within the cell.
F8A1.expression_interpretation: [LOW_EVIDENCE] No expression data available for F8A1 in GTEx.
F8A1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of F8A1 reveals a focused set of associations primarily involving proteins related to coagulation and neuronal functions. Notably, interactions with F8 and its homologs suggest a conserved functional relationship, while the connection with HTT indicates potential links to neurobiological processes. These interactions are characterized by generally high confidence, underscoring their potential biological relevance.

PCDHB5.functional_summary: PCDHB5 functions in calcium ion binding and protein binding, including interactions with cell adhesion molecules, which supports its role in mediating cell adhesion through homophilic cell-cell adhesion mechanisms. It is involved in biological processes such as synapse assembly and chemical synaptic transmission, indicating a role in the formation and function of synaptic connections. Localization to the plasma membrane and synapse is consistent with a role in nervous system development and the establishment of neuronal connectivity. Mechanistic detail is limited by the available annotations.
PCDHB5.expression_interpretation: PCDHB5 shows higher expression in reproductive tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the ovary, testis, uterus, and cervix among the highest-expressing tissues measured. Additionally, notable expression is observed in the pituitary relative to other tissues. This pattern may suggest a role for PCDHB5 in reproductive and endocrine-related functions, although further investigation is required to clarify its biological significance.
PCDHB5.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of PCDHB5 reveals a focused set of associations predominantly with other protocadherin family members, suggesting a role in cell-cell adhesion or signaling within neural contexts. Notably, interactions with PCDHB2, PCDHB11, and PCDHB3 indicate a conserved functional relationship among clustered protocadherins. Additionally, the connection to MYLK3 may reflect a broader regulatory interface, although this interaction warrants further investigation to clarify its biological significance.

biological_processes.name: zinc ion import into synaptic vesicle

TMEM163.functional_summary: TMEM163 functions in zinc ion binding and participates in the transmembrane transport of zinc ions, including their import into synaptic vesicles and export across the plasma membrane, contributing to intracellular zinc ion homeostasis. It is also associated with the biological process of myelination, indicating a potential role in maintaining neuronal function. Localization of TMEM163 to lysosomes, lysosomal membranes, and late endosomes suggests involvement in zinc ion regulation within endocytic and degradative compartments, although mechanistic details remain limited.
TMEM163.expression_interpretation: TMEM163 expression is enriched in specific brain regions within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the cerebellar hemisphere and cerebellum. Additional notable expression occurs in the pituitary, spinal cord (cervical c-1), and frontal cortex (BA9), indicating a pattern of elevated expression in central nervous system tissues relative to others measured. This distribution may suggest a role for TMEM163 in neural or neuroendocrine functions, although further investigation is required to clarify its biological significance.
TMEM163.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of TMEM163 comprises a limited set of partners, indicating a potentially specialized functional role. Notably, interactions with proteins such as ACMSD and TMEM175 suggest involvement in processes related to cellular metabolism and membrane transport. These associations are supported with generally high confidence, underscoring their potential biological relevance.

PCDHA3.functional_summary: PCDHA3 functions in calcium ion binding and interacts with cell adhesion molecules, facilitating cell adhesion processes including homophilic cell-cell adhesion. These activities contribute to nervous system development by promoting the attachment of cells to one another. Localization to the plasma membrane and membrane compartments is consistent with a role in mediating cell-cell interactions at the cell surface.
PCDHA3.expression_interpretation: PCDHA3 shows higher expression in testis relative to other tissues measured within the GTEx dataset, with notable expression also observed in brain regions including the cerebellum and cerebellar hemisphere. Additionally, reproductive tissues such as the uterus and ovary exhibit elevated levels compared to most other tissues. This pattern suggests that PCDHA3 expression is enriched in specific neural and reproductive tissues within the GTEx dataset.
PCDHA3.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of PCDHA3 reveals a focused set of interactions predominantly with other protocadherin alpha family members, suggesting a role in homophilic or closely related heterophilic interactions. These associations are supported with generally high confidence, indicating robust evidence for their biological relevance. This pattern underscores the potential importance of PCDHA3 in mediating cell-cell adhesion processes within neural contexts.

PROKR1.functional_summary: PROKR1 functions as a G protein-coupled receptor that binds extracellular ligands, such as neuropeptides, to initiate intracellular signaling by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP on the alpha subunit of heterotrimeric G-proteins. This activity triggers downstream cellular responses, including those involved in neuropeptide signaling pathways and hormone stimulus responses. Localization of PROKR1 to the plasma membrane is consistent with its role in transducing extracellular signals into intracellular effects. Mechanistic detail beyond these signaling events is limited based on the provided annotations.
PROKR1.expression_interpretation: PROKR1 expression is enriched in specific tissues within the GTEx dataset, with the highest levels observed in the pituitary, followed by testis and visceral adipose tissue. Moderate expression is also detected in breast mammary tissue and the sigmoid colon, while other tissues show comparatively lower levels. This pattern may suggest a role for PROKR1 in endocrine and reproductive tissues, although expression in additional tissues not captured by GTEx cannot be excluded.
PROKR1.interaction_interpretation: The protein interaction network of PROKR1 encompasses 82 interactions, prominently featuring ligands PROK1 and PROK2, which underscores its role in ligand-receptor dynamics. Additional interactions with proteins such as ADCY3 and MRAP2 suggest involvement in signal transduction processes, with several interactions supported by generally high confidence. This network highlights PROKR1's functional connectivity within cellular signaling contexts without implying specific pathway affiliations.
